title: Small AI models let drones autonomously identify and attack battlefield targets
gist: Swedish NATO-backed startup Scaleout Systems, pivoted to defense after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, is deploying small, edge-deployable AI models on drones and forward hardware that use federated learning to keep operating and improving under jamming or lost connectivity, and has already demonstrated a drone autonomously selecting and destroying a target with the BAE Systems Bofors-led ALMA kamikaze-drone program.

insights.claim: Scaleout Systems, founded by Uppsala University researchers in 2018 to deploy machine learning on commercial truck and vehicle hardware, pivoted toward defense applications specifically after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A commercial edge-AI company reorienting entirely toward defense after a geopolitical shock is a pattern investors can expect to recur across European dual-use tech startups as defense spending accelerates.
insights.locator: once Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine

insights.claim: Scaleout's CEO frames the company's mission explicitly as giving NATO allies a strategic advantage by operationalizing edge and sensor data for machine learning, directly tied to the shifting geopolitical environment since 2022.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hellander (quoted)
insights.so_what: Explicit alignment of a startup's mission with NATO strategic advantage signals it is positioned to benefit from continued European defense procurement and NATO innovation funding.
insights.quote: With the war in Ukraine and a shifting world, we realized that this technology can be very important to operationalize edge data and sensor data for machine learning to make sure that NATO allies have found that strategic advantage,
insights.locator: “With the war in Ukraine and a shifting world

insights.claim: Scaleout was selected to join NATO's Defence Innovator Accelerator for the North Atlantic (DIANA) Challenge Program in 2025, where it worked on the Federated Aerial Intelligence for Recon project.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Acceptance into NATO's official innovation accelerator is a validated, trackable signal of institutional backing that could lead to larger procurement contracts.
insights.locator: Scaleout was selected to join NATO’s Defence Innovator

insights.claim: Scaleout deliberately uses lean, small machine learning models for computer vision tasks rather than frontier AI models from OpenAI or Anthropic, because the models must fit on constrained forward-deployed hardware ranging from small embedded devices to more powerful edge workstations.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: This is a concrete counter-narrative to the 'bigger frontier models win' thesis: in latency-, power-, and connectivity-constrained battlefield environments, small specialized models are the commercially and operationally preferred choice, a durable market segment distinct from cloud-scale LLM providers.
insights.locator: Instead of using frontier AI models from OpenAI or Anthropic

themes.theme: Federated learning for resilient, decentralized AI

insights.claim: Scaleout's architecture lets drones and edge devices intermittently share selective model updates with local headquarters computing nodes without transmitting sensitive raw data, and those nodes retrain models on aggregated battlefield data before pushing improved capabilities back to edge devices.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A federated-learning architecture that avoids transmitting raw sensor data is a reusable model for any security-sensitive edge-AI deployment (defense or civilian) where data sovereignty and bandwidth are constraints.
insights.locator: They can then intermittently share selective updates

insights.claim: Scaleout's CEO argues that models trained in one environment (e.g., desert) perform poorly in another (e.g., urban), so the ability to continuously retrain and redeploy updated models during a single day or operation from real-time battlefield sensor data is the company's core sustainable advantage.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hellander (quoted)
insights.so_what: Continuous, environment-specific retraining as a competitive moat is a transferable lesson: static, pre-trained models degrade in novel deployment conditions, making rapid in-field adaptation capability a key value driver over raw model size.
insights.quote: If we can release several new versions of this model that—during the course of a single day or certainly an operation—keep learning and keep improving from this massive amount of sensor data that is generated at a practical edge, that is the sustainable advantage.
insights.locator: Models might have been trained in a desert environment

insights.claim: Relying on a centralized data center to run AI models is increasingly seen as risky given that large data centers have already been targeted and destroyed during the US-Iran war, reinforcing the case for decentralized, locally-running edge AI.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Physical destruction risk to centralized AI data centers during active conflicts is a concrete driver pushing military (and potentially critical civilian) AI infrastructure toward decentralized, edge-resilient architectures.
insights.locator: Reliance on a centralized location to run AI models

insights.claim: Onboard AI capability is critical because electronic warfare and enemy jamming frequently interfere with communication signals on modern battlefields, and a growing number of Ukrainian military drones are already incorporating onboard AI into cheap kamikaze drones.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: Jamming-resilient onboard AI is becoming a baseline requirement for effective drone warfare, evidenced by its adoption trend in Ukraine, and is a capability differentiator defense-tech investors should weight heavily.
insights.locator: This approach is also incredibly useful on modern battlefields

insights.claim: In June, Scaleout tested at a Swedish Air Force base how a forward-deployed computing node could keep running its own AI inference and active-learning processes after losing connection to a central lab node, then sync updates once connectivity was restored.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A live-tested demonstration of graceful degradation and resync under connectivity loss is concrete proof of the resilience claim, relevant for evaluating the technology's real-world readiness versus theoretical capability.
insights.locator: In June, Scaleout also tested its technology

insights.claim: Scaleout is participating in BAE Systems Bofors' Affordable Loitering Modular Ammunition (ALMA) project to develop a low-cost, autonomous kamikaze drone, first publicly demonstrated at a Winter Demo 2026 event in Sweden in January.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A named prime defense contractor (BAE Systems Bofors) partnering with Scaleout on an autonomous munitions program signals real commercial traction beyond R&D demos, relevant for tracking European defense-tech supply chains.
insights.locator: Scaleout is participating in the Affordable Loitering Modular Ammunition

insights.claim: In the ALMA demonstration, a drone autonomously prioritized the highest-value target defined by its mission (an armored engineering vehicle) among multiple detected threats, flew to it, and dropped an explosive on it, with all detection, identification, and geolocation processed entirely onboard without external processing.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: A live demonstration of fully onboard autonomous target prioritization and strike execution (with a human able to still override) marks a concrete operational milestone in autonomous weapons capability worth tracking for policy, ethics, and arms-control debate.
insights.quote: All data is handled by dedicated onboard computing, allowing the system to perform in real-time without any external processing.
insights.locator: That demonstration showed how a drone could autonomously

insights.claim: A human operator retains the ability to control and direct the ALMA drone, but in the demonstrated scenario the drone carried out the target-selection and strike mission on its own without direct human commands.
insights.speaker: Jeremy Hsu
insights.so_what: The human-in-the-loop-but-not-required design pattern illustrates the current operational default for autonomous weapons systems entering deployment, a key detail for tracking the human-control debate in international arms policy.
insights.locator: A human operator could still control and direct the drone

insights.claim: Scaleout's CEO says the federated-learning strategy could eventually scale across entire geographic regions or countries, unlocking collaboration between NATO member states on shared, decentralized AI model improvement.
insights.speaker: Andreas Hellander (quoted)
insights.so_what: A vision of NATO-wide federated defense AI collaboration, if realized, would represent a significant new multinational military-tech infrastructure layer worth monitoring for future funding and procurement announcements.
